DOCUMENT:
Market Analysis: Launching a Digital Subscription for the Calderbrook Courier
Commercial Strategy, Calderbrook Media, April 2026

1. Purpose
The Calderbrook Courier's website is free to read and funded by display advertising, which has declined by about 12% a year for three years. This paper assesses the market for a metered digital subscription, in which readers can view five articles a month free before being asked to subscribe, and recommends a price and launch plan.

2. Our audience
The website had an average of 420,000 monthly unique users (MUU) in 2025, of whom around 60% live in the Courier's circulation area. The printed Courier has 11,200 subscribers paying £18.50 a month for six-day home delivery, plus around 6,000 daily news-stand sales. Print subscribers are older on average than web readers, and most also use the website.

In our March 2026 survey of print subscribers (1,850 responses), 30% said they would cancel their print subscription and take a digital-only subscription instead if one were offered at under £6 a month.

3. Evidence from comparable titles
We obtained data, under confidentiality agreements, from four regional titles that launched metered subscriptions between 2022 and 2024.

Table 1. Comparable regional titles, second year after launch
Title | Monthly unique users | Digital subscribers | Subscribers as % of MUU | Monthly price
Title A | 360,000 | 6,800 | 1.9% | £5.99
Title B | 280,000 | 3,100 | 1.1% | £4.99
Title C | 390,000 | 9,400 | 2.4% | £7.99
Title D | 300,000 | 4,200 | 1.4% | £3.99

All four titles reported that subscriber numbers stabilised by the end of the second year, and that churn settled at between 3% and 5% a month after promotional periods ended.

4. Price
Conversion rates across the comparable titles are highest for the titles charging the lowest prices, which suggests that our audience will respond best to a low price point. We therefore propose a price of £4.99 a month, with an introductory offer of £1 for the first three months.

5. Projection
The average conversion rate of the four comparable titles is 2.0% of MUU. Applied to our 420,000 MUU, that gives about 8,400 subscribers by the end of year two. At £4.99 a month, 8,400 subscribers would generate around £503,000 a year in subscription revenue.

Table 2. Year-two projection
Item | Annual amount
Subscription revenue | £503,000
Subscription platform and payment fees | £85,000
Marketing | £60,000
Net contribution | £358,000

We expect a modest reduction in display advertising revenue as page views from non-subscribers fall when they reach the meter; the comparable titles reported falls of 5% to 8% in page views. Our display revenue was £1.1 million in 2025, so a fall of this size would cost between £55,000 and £88,000 a year, which is well covered by the projected net contribution.

6. Launch plan
- Platform selection and integration: May to July 2026.
- Soft launch with a ten-article meter: September 2026.
- Full launch with a five-article meter: November 2026.
- Review of price and meter after six months.

7. Conclusion
The evidence from comparable titles shows a viable market for a Courier digital subscription. At £4.99 a month, a price that the comparable titles' experience suggests will maximise take-up, we project around 8,400 subscribers and a net contribution of £358,000 a year, more than offsetting the expected effect on display advertising. We recommend approval to proceed with the launch plan.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [arithmetic] at: "The average conversion rate of the four comparable titles is 2.0% of MUU." -- (1.9 + 1.1 + 2.4 + 1.4) / 4 = 1.7%, not 2.0%. At 1.7% the projection is about 7,140 subscribers, not 8,400, and revenue about £428,000.
2. [misread_evidence] at: "Conversion rates across the comparable titles are highest for the titles charging the lowest prices" -- Table 1 shows the opposite pattern: the highest-priced title (C, £7.99) has the highest conversion (2.4%) and the lowest-priced (D, £3.99) has 1.4%. The pricing rationale rests on misreading the table.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "At £4.99 a month, 8,400 subscribers would generate around £503,000 a year in subscription revenue." -- The projection treats all subscription revenue as incremental, but the document's own survey says 30% of the 11,200 print subscribers (about 3,360) would cancel £18.50 print subscriptions for a digital one under £6. Switching would cost about £13.51 a month each (roughly £545,000 a year), which is never addressed although it could wipe out the net contribution.

REVIEW:
# Review: Digital Subscription Market Analysis, Calderbrook Courier

The paper is clearly structured, and using confidential regional comparables instead of national benchmarks is the right approach. However, the comparables table doesn't support two of the paper's central claims, and the biggest financial risk isn't costed at all. With those corrected, the case as written doesn't hold.

## Major issues

### 1. The average conversion rate is 1.7%, not 2.0%

From Table 1: (1.9 + 1.1 + 2.4 + 1.4) / 4 = **1.7%**. Weighting by audience size (23,500 subscribers ÷ 1,330,000 MUU) gives 1.77%.

At 1.7%, the projection falls from 8,400 to about **7,140 subscribers**. Revenue falls from £503,000 to about **£428,000**. Everything downstream, including Table 2, the display-revenue comparison and the conclusion, needs recalculating.

### 2. The data contradicts the pricing rationale

Section 4 says conversion is highest where price is lowest. Table 1 shows roughly the opposite:

| Price | Title | Conversion |
|---|---|---|
| £7.99 | C | **2.4%** (highest) |
| £5.99 | A | 1.9% |
| £4.99 | B | **1.1%** (lowest) |
| £3.99 | D | 1.4% |

The highest-priced title converts best, and the title at our proposed £4.99 converts worst. With four data points and obvious confounders (content, meter design, local competition), these figures don't prove that higher prices convert better. They certainly don't show that a low price maximises take-up. The £4.99 recommendation therefore has no evidential basis in the paper.

Price also matters more than the paper assumes. If Title A's 1.9% is achievable at £5.99, revenue would be about 20% higher than at £4.99 with similar volume.

### 3. Print cannibalisation is not costed, and it likely outweighs the gain

Section 2 reports that 30% of print subscribers would switch to digital-only below £6. The proposed £4.99 price triggers exactly that, but Section 5 never accounts for it.

- 30% × 11,200 = **3,360 switchers**
- Each moves from £18.50 to £4.99, a loss of £13.51 a month
- 3,360 × £13.51 × 12 = **about £545,000 a year** in lost revenue

That exceeds even the paper's overstated £358,000 net contribution. Stated survey intent usually overstates behaviour, but even if only a third switched (about 1,100), the loss would be about £180,000.

Savings on printing and delivery for lost copies would offset some of this. They need to be estimated, not left out. This is the most important gap: the author's summary says the display loss is "explicitly costed," but the larger and more predictable loss is not. The paper should also consider whether switchers count toward the 7,140–8,400 figure. If they do, fewer of those subscribers are genuinely new revenue.

### 4. The revenue line ignores the introductory offer and churn

- **Introductory offer.** New subscribers pay £1 for three months. With churn of 3–5% a month, a base of about 7,000 loses roughly 250–350 subscribers a month. Replacing them means 3,000–4,000 new subscribers a year on the £1 offer. That costs roughly £35,000–£50,000 a year against full-price revenue.
- **Ramp-up.** Table 2 is labelled a year-two projection, but it applies the *end*-of-year-two subscriber count to the *whole* year. Average year-two subscribers will be lower, so year-two revenue is overstated. Year one, with its integration costs, isn't shown at all.

## Smaller points

- **Audience mix.** Only 60% of our MUU are in the circulation area. If the comparables have a more local audience, applying their conversion rate to our total MUU overstates take-up. Our 420,000 MUU is also above every comparable, so we are extrapolating beyond the range of the data.
- **The soft launch is too short to learn from.** Two months on a ten-article meter can't reveal stable conversion or churn, which the comparables say take up to two years to settle. The plan also sets no go/no-go criteria, such as the conversion, churn or print-cancellation levels that would trigger a rethink. Without these, the phased launch doesn't really let us "learn before committing fully."
- **Timeline.** The paper is dated April 2026 and puts full launch in November 2026. If it's being reviewed now, the dates need updating.
- **The display-loss calculation is arithmetically correct** (£55,000–£88,000). With display revenue falling about 12% a year, it may be slightly high by year two. That is a minor point in the paper's favour.

## Indicative corrected position (year two, steady state)

| Item | Paper | Revised (approx.) |
|---|---|---|
| Subscribers | 8,400 | 7,140 |
| Subscription revenue | £503,000 | £428,000 |
| Intro-offer discount | not included | −£35,000 to −£50,000 |
| Platform and payment fees (~17%) | −£85,000 | −£70,000 |
| Marketing | −£60,000 | −£60,000 |
| **Net contribution** | **£358,000** | **about £250,000–£265,000** |
| Display revenue loss | −£55,000 to −£88,000 | −£55,000 to −£88,000 |
| Print cannibalisation (net of digital price) | not included | −£180,000 to −£545,000, before print cost savings |

On these figures, the overall effect ranges from roughly break-even to clearly negative. The outcome depends mostly on how many print subscribers switch.

## Recommendations before resubmitting

1. Correct the average to 1.7% and recalculate throughout.
2. Remove the claim that low prices maximise take-up. Present price scenarios (£4.99, £5.99, £7.99) instead.
3. Model print cannibalisation explicitly, including print cost savings, under a range of switching rates. Consider pricing or bundling that protects print, such as digital included with print or a digital price closer to print.
4. Build a month-by-month model that includes churn, the introductory offer and ramp-up, covering both years.
5. Set measurable criteria for the soft launch and the six-month review.

The opportunity may well be real. As written, though, the paper overstates the upside, misreads its own price evidence and omits the largest downside risk.
